messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Vikram, a forty-four-year-old South Asian American who had built his life around the controlled chaos of professional kitchens, remembered the collapse not as a story he could tell, but as a series of weightless, unspoken fragments that refused to settle into language. When the past surfaced, he could mechanically reconstruct the rubble, yet the emotions remained entirely absent, as though he were watching a film of a stranger’s suffering. The sheer impossibility of what he had witnessed, combined with his own unblemished skin upon extraction, quickly hardened into a rigid conviction that he was permanently damaged and carried a debt of guilt for those who perished. This heavy, unyielding judgment of his own survival and his perceived moral failure became the lens through which he viewed the present. Because he believed he was fundamentally broken and burdened by what he had not done, the sharp wail of an approaching ambulance or a radio broadcast detailing a highway pileup instantly pulled him back into the past, forcing the trauma to overwrite his current reality. When those sirens cut through his day or a coworker leaned in to discuss a friend’s crash, his nervous system immediately snapped into a state of hyperalertness, his concentration fracturing as he instinctively began charting every available exit before he could even steady his breathing. This relentless scanning and mental exhaustion compelled him to adopt rigid rules of engagement. He found himself deliberately routing his commutes away from open plazas where he felt exposed, and when confronted with sudden tension or authority figures, he would immediately soften his posture, agreeing to every request just to keep the perceived danger from spiraling. By constantly retreating into submission and confined spaces, he inadvertently confirmed his own worst fears, reinforcing the conviction that he had been irreparably altered by the event and that his only chance of safety lay in total deference. The conviction of permanent damage and inaction guilt also amplified his baseline alarm, making every unexpected noise feel like a prelude to inevitable harm, while his belief that he was fundamentally compromised pushed him toward a posture of extreme deference whenever stress surfaced. This persistent pattern of hiding and yielding created a feedback loop that calcified over months. Because he refused to tolerate unpredictable environments, ordinary kitchen sounds became magnified, instantly drawing his gaze to any potential injury or emergency vehicle nearby. His constant flight and compliance only deepened his baseline alarm, transforming his open prep area into a perimeter he had to defensively map, which in turn made the traumatic recall fracture into even more detached, emotionless snapshots that felt increasingly impossible to process. The exhaustion of perpetual vigilance further eroded his capacity to ground the past, leaving those wordless flashes trapped in his chest. Over time, this cycle cost him his social life; he stopped taking breaks with his line cooks, finding the exposed dining hall too exposing, and his silence at staff meetings drew concerned glances he interpreted as further proof of his isolation. The sheer weight of carrying those silent debts while navigating a world that suddenly felt full of invisible tripwires finally pushed him through the clinic doors. He was terrified that his career would become an inescapable crime scene of his own making, yet he desperately hoped someone might help him untangle the guilt from his survival, so he could finally stop bracing for a collapse that had already passed.
